'''Ali Al-Tamimi''' (also '''Ali Al-Timimi'''; born December 14, 1963) is an American [[Computational biology|computational biologist]] and Islamic teacher from [[Fairfax County, Virginia]], who was convicted of [[Solicitation|soliciting]] [[treason]] and attempting to contribute services to the [[Taliban]] based on comments he is alleged to have made to a group of followers at a private dinner shortly after [[9/11]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite news|last=Lichtblau|first=Eric|date=2005-07-14|title=Scholar Is Given Life Sentence in 'Virginia Jihad' Case|language=en-US|work=The New York Times|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2005/07/14/us/scholar-is-given-life-sentence-in-virginia-jihad-case.html|access-date=2020-07-27|issn=0362-4331}}</ref><ref name="mark">{{cite news|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/article/2005/07/13/AR2005071302169.html|title=Muslim Lecturer Sentenced To Life; Followers Trained For Armed Jihad|last=Markon|first=Jerry|date=July 14, 2005|access-date=March 3, 2010 | newspaper=The Washington Post}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|author=Mounir al Mawry|date=July 15, 2005|title=Loading|url=http://aawsat.com/english/news.asp?id=829&section=1|access-date=March 6, 2010|publisher=Aawsat.com}}{{Dead link|date=August 2023 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.usatoday.com/news/nation/2004-02-13-terror-paintball_x.htm |title=Terror defendant allegedly trained for Taliban after 9/11 |work=USA Today |date=February 13, 2004 |access-date=March 6, 2010}}</ref> He was subsequently sentenced to life in prison in 2005.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.courtlistener.com/docket/4608498/united-states-v-al-timimi/|title=United States v. Al-Timimi, 1:04-cr-00385 - CourtListener.com|website=CourtListener}}</ref> Al-Timimi was held in solitary confinement for more than fifteen years including over a decade under [[Special administrative measure|special administrative measures]] at the [[Supermax prison|maximum security]] [[United States Penitentiary Administrative Maximum Facility|United States Penitentiary ADX Florence]], [[Colorado]]. In August 2020, the district court ordered his [[conditional release]] into [[House arrest|home confinement]] pending appeal after concluding that his case raised substantial legal issues.<ref name=":7" /><ref>{{Cite news |date=2020-08-18 |title=Islamic scholar ordered released while appeal is pursued |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/local/islamic-scholar-ordered-released-while-appeal-is-pursued/2020/08/18/697145c6-e187-11ea-82d8-5e55d47e90ca_story.html |access-date=2024-01-27 |newspaper=Washington Post |language=en-US |issn=0190-8286}}</ref> His direct appeal was filed on August 1, 2025 in the Fourth Circuit after twenty years in the district court,<ref>{{Cite web | title=United States v. Ali Al-Timimi, 14-4451 – CourtListener.com | url=https://www.courtlistener.com/docket/67420780/united-states-v-ali-al-timimi/ | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250910023908/https://www.courtlistener.com/docket/67420780/united-states-v-ali-al-timimi/ | access-date=2026-09-28 | archive-date=2025-09-10}}</ref> and in January 2026 his conviction was overturned on [[First Amendment to the United States Constitution|First Amendment]] grounds.<ref name=Politico>{{Cite news|URL=https://www.politico.com/news/2026/01/09/court-sept-11-convictions-first-amendment-00719327|title=Court throws out Sept.11-era convictions on First Amendment grounds|work=Politico|date=9 January 2026|access-date=11 January 2026}}</ref>

==Early life and education==
Al-Timimi was born in 1963 and grew up in the [[The Palisades (Washington, D.C.)|Palisades]] neighborhood of [[Washington, D.C.|Washington, DC]], where he attended [[Georgetown Day School]] until age fifteen.<ref name=":3">Milton Viorst, [https://www.theatlantic.com/magazine/archive/2006/06/the-education-of-ali-al-timimi/304884/ "The Education of Ali Al-Timimi"], ''The Atlantic'', June 2006; retrieved June 9, 2019.</ref><ref name="mark"/><ref name=":4">{{Cite book|last=Heffelfinger|first=Chris|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=nh54E_Ni_x8C&q=georgetown+day+school+ali+al-timimi&pg=PT103|title=Radical Islam in America: Salafism's Journey from Arabia to the West|date=2011|publisher=Potomac Books, Inc.|isbn=978-1-59797-603-9|language=en}}</ref> His father (d. 2010), an attorney, was the [[cultural attaché]] at the embassy of the then [[Kingdom of Iraq]]. His mother, a mental health specialist with a doctorate in special education, initially taught at [[St. John's Episcopal Church, Lafayette Square|St. John's Child Development Center]] for [[Intellectual disability|intellectually disabled]] children. Later in the mid-1970s, she was a dean at [[Mount Vernon Seminary and College|Mt. Vernon College for Women]].<ref name=":3" />

One of Al-Timimi's teenage friends was the son of journalist [[Milton Viorst]], who later wrote in ''[[The Atlantic]]'' that the family was "not particularly ethnic or religious," and that Al-Timimi celebrated holidays such as Halloween and Christmas with his brother and other friends at school.<ref name=":3" /> Viorst writes that Al-Timimi's parents were both practicing Muslims, but spoke English rather than Arabic at home and "did not push religious observance on the children."<ref name=":3" />

At age fifteen, in 1978, Al-Timimi's parents moved the family to [[Riyadh]], Saudi Arabia for three years to expose them to their Arabic and Islamic heritage. Al-Timimi attended Manarat Riyadh High School, where he learned [[Arabic]] and studied [[Islam]] under [[Bilal Philips|Bilal Phillips]].<ref name=":4" /> In Saudi Arabia, Al-Timimi became influenced by [[Salafi movement|Salafism]], a reform branch of [[Sunni Islam]] that advocates strict adherence to the [[Quran]] and [[Sunnah|Sunna]] (the teachings of the Prophet).<ref name=":4" /><ref name=":3" />

In 1981, Al-Timimi returned to the United States and enrolled in a [[Pre-medical|premed]] program at [[George Washington University|The George Washington University]], while spending much of his time networking with different groups in the local Muslim community. Al-Timimi was quoted as saying that he "flirted with each group, only quickly to become disinterested in their rhetoric and what I perceived as their being out of touch with the questions being raised in America—about Islam and the Muslims."<ref name=":3" />

==Intellectual influences==
Stating that he was "hungry for answers to the larger philosophical questions," Al-Timimi returned to Saudi Arabia in 1987, where he studied for a year at the [[Islamic University of Madinah]] and became a student of [[Abd al-Aziz ibn Baz|Abdul-Aziz bin Baz]].<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":4" />  [[Michael Sells]] who has investigated Al-Timimi's belief system has written, "It is Bin Baz’s understanding of Islam, in fact, that ... guides central assumptions within Timimi’s speeches." He also stated, "Were we to name the militant interpretation ... found in Timimi’s speech, then, we might call it Bin Bazism."<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Sells |first=Michael |date=December 2006 |title=War as Worship, Worship as War |url=https://www.islamicpluralism.org/documents/367.pdf |journal=The Religion and Culture Web Forum |pages=12, 17 |access-date=January 1, 2024}}</ref>

Al-Timimi also became influenced by [[Islamist]] thinkers like [[Sayyid Qutb]], [[Abd al-Rahman Abd al-Khaliq]], [[Safar Al-Hawali]] and [[Muhammad Surur]].<ref name="Hitchens">Alexander Meleagrou-Hitchens, ''Salafism in America: History, Evolution, Radicalization'', October 2018, p. 67. Report for the George Washington University Program on Extremism. [https://extremism.gwu.edu/sites/g/files/zaxdzs2191/f/Salafism%20in%20America.pdf Link].</ref><ref name=":5">{{Cite book|last=Bowen|first=Innes|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=XhcoBgAAQBAJ|title=Medina in Birmingham, Najaf in Brent: Inside British Islam|date=2014-08-15|publisher=Hurst|isbn=9781849045308}}</ref><ref name=":8">{{Cite book |last1=Marquardt |first1=Erich |url=https://www.aclu.org/wp-content/uploads/legal-documents/ACLURM000540.pdf |title=Terrorism & Political Islam Origins, Ideologies, and Methods: A Counterterrorism Textbook |last2=Heffelfinger |first2=Christopher |edition=2nd |pages=265, 390}}</ref> Following his April 2005 conviction, an editorial about Al-Timimi's life appeared in the Saudi newspaper [[Al Madina (newspaper)|Al Madina]]. It described his "personality as one that combines eloquence, steadfastness in times of adversity, and unique opinions from one angle, with gentleness and a good community spirit from another angle. I was very impressed with this unique mix that made me see him as being similar to the martyr Sayyid Qutb."<ref>{{Cite news |last=Alim |first=Bassim A. |orig-date=April 29, 2005 |title=صناعة الحياة |trans-title=Forged by Life |url=https://www.somaliaonline.com/community/topic/4889-ali-al-tamimi-an-embodiment-of-faith/ |access-date=January 1, 2024 |work=Al Madina |location=Jeddah, Saudi Arabia |page=19 |language=Arabic |issue=15346}}</ref> 

At his parents' urging, Al-Timimi returned to the United States after a year of study and earned a second undergraduate degree in computer science from the [[University of Maryland, College Park|University of Maryland]]. He later earned a Ph.D. in [[computational biology]] from [[George Mason University]] in 2004, after defending his [[Thesis|doctoral thesis]] titled "Chaos and Complexity in Cancer."<ref name=":4" /> His doctoral thesis reflected, in large part, the influence of the ideas of [[Harold J. Morowitz|Harold Morowitz]], one of his professors, on his thinking.

An FBI assessment of Al-Timimi noted that "[d]espite (Al-Timimi's) early attachment to [Bin Baz], he was open to rational methods (bin Baz famously insisted the world was flat in a 1976 fatwa) and continued his pursuit of science, eventually defending his PhD dissertation at George Mason University in Virginia in computational biology."<ref name=":8" />

==Employment==
As an IT specialist, Al-Timimi worked at an IT company named Xpedior, Inc. Clients he provided service to included [[AOL|America Online]] (AOL). He reportedly worked for two months for [[Andrew Card]], while he was [[United States Secretary of Transportation|Secretary of Transportation]] under [[George H. W. Bush]] (1992–93).

As a scientific researcher, Al-Timimi worked for the United States Navy and at George Mason University where he held the rank of [[Assistant professor|Assistant Professor]].<ref name=":3" />

==Islamic activities==
After returning from [[Medina]], Al-Timimi began to deliver lectures on [[Salafi movement|Salafiyya]] at Islamic conferences throughout the 1990s, and gradually developed an audience.<ref name=":4" /> Dozens of his lectures have been published on the internet.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://archive.org/details/1.AddressToTheAudience | title=Ali Tamimi Lectures }}</ref> [[Milton Viorst|Viorst]] writes that Al-Timimi avoided contemporaneous political issues, but instead reflected on "the Islamic vision of [[Judgement Day in Islam|Judgment Day]], prophecy, the nature of the [[Traditionalist theology (Islam)|divine]], and ''[[fiqh]]'' (Islamic jurisprudence)—subjects with which he grappled in Medina and in his private reading."<ref name=":3" />

In the late 1990s, he cofounded an Islamic center in [[Falls Church, Virginia]] with his mentor, the Sudanese Islamic scholar Jaafar Sheikh Idris, which they named Dar al-Arqam.<ref name=":3" /> Al-Timimi became its primary lecturer, and delivered weekly lessons on Salafiyya to approximately a hundred attendees a week.<ref name=":3" /><ref name="mark"/> According to Umar Lee, Al-Timimi's lectures "became 'the place to be' for the youth of the masjids [mosques] throughout the D.C. area," who were attracted to the fact that "this was a man who was born and raised in America, spoke in clear English, and not only had a great knowledge of the ''[[Din (Arabic)|dīn]]'' (religion) but was college educated, a cancer researcher, and a very serious intellectual. This was a man who could take the knowledge of the [[Salaf]] and make it applicable to your everyday life and could speak in a language we all understood."<ref name=":4" /> 

In 1995, Al-Timimi led a five-person delegation from the Islamic Assembly of North America to the [[United Nations]] [[World Conference on Women, 1995|4th World Conference on Women]], held in [[Beijing]], China.<ref name=":3" /> Al-Timimi also translated into English a book about [[women in Islam]] that was written by [[Abd al-Rahman Abd al-Khaliq|Abdel Rahman Abdel Khaliq]].<ref>{{cite web|title=THE WISDOM BEHIND THE ISLAMIC LAWS REGARDING WOMEN {{!}} Al Huda Islamic Center of Athens|url=https://www.athensislamiccenter.org/node/271|access-date=2020-08-01|website=athensislamiccenter.org}}</ref>

Al-Timimi has been characterized as "arguably the first American born activist [[Salafi]] preacher."<ref name="Hitchens" /> 

==Awlaki visit==
In October 2002, the former [[Dar al-Hijrah]] imam [[Anwar al-Awlaki]] visited Al-Timimi and inquired about recruiting men for "violent jihad."<ref name="wash post">Schmidt, Susan; [https://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/article/2008/02/26/AR2008022603267.html Imam From Va. Mosque Now Thought to Have Aided Al-Qaeda]; ''The Washington Post'', February 27, 2008. pg. 3. Retrieved November 20, 2009.</ref><ref name="how">{{cite news|url=https://abcnews.go.com/Blotter/FtHoodInvestigation/anwar-awlaki/story?id=9200720&page=3|last=Rhee|first=Joseph|date=November 30, 2009|title=How Anwar Awlaki Got Away; U.S. Attorney's Decision to Cancel Arrest Warrant "Shocked" Terrorism Investigators|work= ABC News|access-date=December 1, 2009}}</ref> But Al-Timimi became suspicious of al-Awlaki's motives, believing it to be an entrapment attempt and asked al-Awlaki to leave.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Dirty Wars: The World Is A Battlefield|last=Scahill|first=Jeremy|publisher=Nation Books|year=2013|isbn=978-1568586717|location=London, UK|page=71|quote="Why was the guy [al-Awlaki] there? Why was he asking somebody he'd never met in his whole life to help him get young men for the jihad? It just stunk of entrapment. Ali threw him out of the house."}}</ref> In a Tweet on August 18, 2020, CBS national security correspondent, [[Catherine Herridge]] argued that the entire case was motivated by the Awlaki visit to Al-Timimi's home.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2021-10-24 |title=FBI incompetence let Anwar al Awlaki slip away, say retired investigators |url=https://news.yahoo.com/fbi-incompetence-let-anwar-al-110000576.html |access-date=2024-01-27 |website=Yahoo News |language=en-US |quote="What the investigators did not know was that Ammerman was overseeing a separate terror investigation into what became known as the 'Virginia Paintball' case. A cancer researcher and self-described Muslim scholar named Dr. Ali al-Timimi had allegedly inspired a group of young men from Virginia who used paintball to train for holy war to go to Pakistan to join the terror organization Lashkar-e-Taiba. Al-Awlaki was working as an informant for the FBI in that case, and nabbing him for 9/11 would blow his cover, the two investigators later discovered."}}</ref>

==Trial and sentencing==
Prior to Al-Timimi's prosecution, a group of young Muslim men that prosecutors described as a "[[Virginia jihad network|Virginia Jihad Network]]" were convicted on charges related to their travels to a militant training camp in Pakistan called [[Lashkar-e-Taiba]],<ref name=":1">{{cite web|last=Barakat|first=Matthew|date=2017-04-20|title=Bosnia to Pakistan to prison: Ex-fighter reflects on life|url=https://apnews.com/41c1908d5a0d410ca85a23cbdd85f871|access-date=2020-07-27|website=AP NEWS}}</ref> a group that the United States would later designate as a [[United States Department of State list of Foreign Terrorist Organizations|Foreign Terrorist Organization]] on December 26, 2001.<ref>{{cite web|title=Amendments to the Terrorist Designation of Lashkar e-Tayyiba|url=https://www.state.gov/amendments-to-the-terrorist-designation-of-lashkar-e-tayyiba/|access-date=2020-07-27|website=United States Department of State|language=en-US}}</ref> Al-Timimi was named as an [[unindicted co-conspirator]] in that case.<ref name="mark"/>  According to prosecutors, Al-Timimi told his followers at a private gathering on September 16, 2001, that he believed that the [[September 11 attacks|9/11 attacks]] had been an omen that foreshadowed a looming end-of-times battle between Muslims and the West,<ref name=":2">{{Cite news|last=Barakat|first=Matthew|date=2019-06-25|title=Islamic scholar's terror convictions reviewed in Virginia|language=en-US|agency=Associated Press|url=https://abcnews.go.com/US/wireStory/islamic-scholars-terror-convictions-reviewed-virginia-63932671|access-date=2020-07-27}}</ref> and that "the time had come for them to go abroad and join the [[Mujahideen|mujaheddin]] engaged in violent jihad in Afghanistan."<ref name="mark"/><ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ja53Ai6IcYwC&q=%22the+time+had+come+for+them+to+go+abroad+and+join+the%22&pg=PA124 |title=''The Next Attack: The Failure of the War on Terror and a Strategy for Getting It Right'', Daniel Benjamin, Steven Simon, Macmillan, 2006, ISBN 0-8050-8133-X, accessed March 3, 2010 |date=September 11, 2001 |isbn=9780805081336 |access-date=April 29, 2010|last1=Benjamin |first1=Daniel |last2=Simon |first2=Steven |publisher=Macmillan }}</ref> Another attendee at the gathering, Randall Royer, advised the men that they could receive military training from Lashkar-e-Taiba, and put the men in contact with the group.<ref name=":1" /> Several of the attendees went on to travel to Lashkar-e-Taiba and participate in military training exercises, though none ultimately did any fighting.<ref name=":2" /> FBI Special Agent Tim Ervin described the Virginia Jihad prosecution before the [[9/11 Commission]] as follows: "The [[Buffalo Six|Lackawanna 6]] was a good case. The other prosecutions for terrorism are B.S. They would never have investigated the Virginia jihad group before 9/11".<ref>{{cite book | url=https://catalog.archives.gov/id/2610080 | title=Memorandum for the Record (MFR) of the Interview of Tim Ervin of the Federal Bureau of Investigation Conducted by Team 1A | series=Series: Memorandums for the Record, 1928 - 2007 | date=October 17, 2003 }}</ref>

After the conclusion of the Virginia Jihad Network trials, prosecutors tried Al-Timimi for helping to inspire their travel to Lashkar-e-Taiba.<ref name=":2" /><ref name="mark"/>  The case was tried before U.S. District Judge [[Leonie M. Brinkema]] in the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia|Eastern District of Virginia]], and charged Al-Timimi with 10 criminal counts, including solicitation of treason<ref name=":0" /> and attempting to aid the [[Taliban]].<ref name=":0" /><ref name="mark"/>  Al-Timimi's defense lawyers argued his case was an attack on the [[Freedom of speech in the United States|freedom of speech]] and [[Freedom of religion in the United States|religious freedom]], arguing that their client only told young Muslims that it might be better to emigrate from the United States to better practice their faith.<ref>{{cite news| url= http://www.democracynow.org/2005/7/14/headlines|last=Goodman|first=Amy |date=July 14, 2005|title= HEADLINES JULY 14, 2005|work= Democracy Now |access-date=March 18, 2015}}</ref>

After a week of deliberation, the jury found Al-Timimi guilty of all 10 counts in April 2005.<ref name="mark"/>  At a sentencing hearing on July 14, 2005, he received a [[Mandatory sentencing|mandatory lifetime prison sentence]].<ref name="mark"/> Judge Brinkema described the sentence as "very draconian,"<ref name=":0" /> but said "I don't think any well-read person can doubt the truth that terrorist camps are a crucial part of the new terrorism that is perpetrated in the world today. People of good will need to do whatever they can to stop that."<ref name="mark"/>[https://www.courtlistener.com/docket/4608498/united-states-v-al-timimi/ United States v. Al-Timimi, 1:04-cr-00385 - CourtListener.com]

At sentencing, Al-Timimi "made an eloquent statement to the court, quoting from the Constitution and Socrates. [He] pointed out that he had 'never owned or used a gun, never traveled to a military camp, never set foot in a country in which a war was taking place, never raised money for any violent organization.' For his conviction to stand, he said: '[T]wo hundred and thirty years of America's tradition of protecting the individual from the tyrannies and whims of the sovereign will have come to an end. And that which is exploited today to persecute a single member of a minority will most assuredly come back to haunt the majority tomorrow.'"<ref>{{cite journal |last1= Freivogel |first1= W. H.| date= 2007| title= Tom Eagleton and 'the Curse to our Constitution'.| url= https://scholarship.law.slu.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1652&context=lj| journal= St. Louis University Law Journal| volume= 52| issue= 1| pages= 131–132| doi= | access-date= 2022-11-10}}</ref>

Royer was released from prison in December 2016, and now works for a nonprofit group that seeks to undermine religious extremism.<ref>{{cite web|last=Khan|first=Nushmia|title=This man spent 14 years in prison with terrorists and is now fighting extremism|url=https://qz.com/989106/this-man-spent-14-years-in-prison-with-terrorists-like-the-unabomber-and-is-now-fighting-extremism/|access-date=2020-08-01|website=Quartz|date=May 23, 2017 |language=en}}</ref> Since his release, Royer has maintained that "Timimi did not specifically say join the Taliban or help al-Qaeda though he seemed to imply it."<ref>{{cite web|last=Ismail|first=Royer|date=July 20, 2019|url=https://twitter.com/ismailroyer/status/1152714483611176960|access-date=2020-08-01|website=Twitter|language=en}}</ref> However, Royer has also said that Al-Timimi's statement that Muslim men should "go be with the mujahideen" was "colossally bad advice."<ref>{{cite web|title=Bosnia to Pakistan to Prison: Ex-Fighter Reflects on Life|url=https://www.voanews.com/usa/bosnia-pakistan-prison-ex-fighter-reflects-life|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191031002106/https://www.voanews.com/usa/bosnia-pakistan-prison-ex-fighter-reflects-life|url-status=dead|archive-date=October 31, 2019|access-date=2020-08-01|website=Voice of America|language=en}}</ref>

==Appeals==
In late 2005, Al-Timimi's appellate attorneys sought discovery on whether Al-Timimi had been subjected to illegal wiretaps in light of the then-recently disclosed [[NSA warrantless surveillance (2001–07)|NSA warrantless surveillance]] program.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2005-dec-29-na-spy29-story.html|title=Lawyers Question Use of U.S. Spy Program|work=Los Angelest Times, Associated Press|date=December 29, 2006|access-date=March 1, 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.onthemedia.org/story/128866-tap-dance/transcript|title=Tap Dance|work=National Public Radio|date=January 20, 2006|access-date=March 1, 2016|author=Carr, Rick|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160306205725/http://www.onthemedia.org/story/128866-tap-dance/transcript|archive-date=March 6, 2016|url-status=dead}}</ref> The [[United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit|U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit]] responded by remanding the case back to the district court, giving broad latitude to the trial judge. The [[United States Department of Justice|Justice Department]] did not confirm or deny the use of NSA wiretaps against Al-Timimi.<ref>{{cite news|title=Cleric Wins Appeal Ruling Over Wiretaps|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2006/04/26/washington/26terror.html| work=New York Times|date=April 26, 2006|access-date=March 1, 2016|author=Lichtblau, Eric}}</ref>

In 2006, Al-Timimi's attorneys also challenged his treatment by the [[Federal Bureau of Prisons]], claiming that it had repeatedly moved him to new facilities to block him from meeting with his legal counsel. Attorney [[Jonathan Turley]] told [[NPR]] that Al-Timimi "was transferred to at least six different prisons in four states in less than six months. It became a version of Where's Waldo. We could not find him."<ref name=":6">{{cite web|author=Inskeep, Steve|date=August 16, 2006|title=Islamic Scholar Challenges Treatment in Prison|url=https://www.npr.org/templates/story/story.php?storyId=5656297|access-date=March 1, 2016|work=National Public Radio}}</ref> After an internal investigation, BOP found that a prison official had "verbally harassed" Al-Timimi, but concluded that it had insufficient evidence to substantiate Al-Timimi's other claims.<ref name=":6" />

In September 2015, the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit|Fourth Circuit]] again [[Remand (court procedure)|remanded]] the case, this time on the grounds that "the FBI withheld evidence of its 2002 investigation into the first American on the CIA's [[Disposition Matrix|kill or capture list]], [[Anwar al-Awlaki]]".<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.foxnews.com/politics/circuit-court-remands-terrorism-case-on-grounds-fbi-withheld-info-of-al-awlaki-investigation/|title=Circuit court remands terrorism case on grounds FBI withheld info of al-Awlaki investigation|work=Fox News|date=September 26, 2015|access-date=March 1, 2016|author1=Browne, Pamela K.|author2=Herridge Catherine}}</ref>

Between 2016 and 2019, Al-Timimi's attorneys further argued that several of his convictions have been rendered invalid by the [[Supreme Court of the United States|Supreme Court]]'s intervening decisions in ''[[Johnson v. United States (2015)|Johnson v. United States]]'' and ''[[United States v. Davis (2019)|United States v. Davis]]''.<ref>{{Cite news|last=Weiner|first=Rachel|title='Fuzzy' language in law leads to reversals in gun cases|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/local/legal-issues/fuzzy-language-in-law-leads-to-reversals-in-gun-cases/2018/12/28/88374154-fe2b-11e8-ad40-cdfd0e0dd65a_story.html|access-date=2020-08-01|newspaper=Washington Post|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|date=2019-06-25|title=Islamic scholar's terror convictions reviewed in Virginia|url=https://federalnewsnetwork.com/government-news/2019/06/islamic-scholars-terror-convictions-reviewed-in-virginia/|access-date=2020-08-01|website=Federal News Network|language=en-US}}</ref>

On April 27, 2020, Al-Timimi's attorneys filed a motion for his conditional release from prison pending the remainder of his appeal, arguing that intervening Supreme Court authority had cast doubt on the charges that continued to subject him to imprisonment, and that the [[COVID-19 pandemic|COVID-19]] pandemic additionally presented an exceptional reason justifying his release.<ref name=":7">{{cite web|last=Katkov|first=Mark|title=Judge Orders Release, During Appeal, Of Man Convicted Post-9/11 Of Soliciting Treason|url=https://www.npr.org/2020/08/19/903793682/judge-orders-release-of-virginia-terror-convict-pending-appeal|access-date=2020-08-23|website=NPR.org|date=August 19, 2020 |language=en}}</ref>

On August 18, 2020, Judge Brinkema granted the motion and ordered Al-Timimi's [[conditional release]] from [[ADX Florence|ADX]] and into [[House arrest|home confinement]] while he pursues his appeal.<ref>{{cite web|last=Barakat|first=Matthew|date=2020-08-18|title=Islamic scholar ordered released while appeal is pursued|url=https://apnews.com/69644a163982bd2af8b565bf19b29ec0|access-date=2020-08-19|website=AP NEWS}}</ref> On September 1, 2020, Al-Timimi was released from ADX Florence and placed into home confinement.

On July 18, 2024, Judge Brinkema overturned three of the 10 counts on which he was convicted, including his life sentence. "But she upheld other counts that could leave him with decades of prison time beyond the 15 years he already served ... She also rejected allegations that prosecutors failed to disclose information that the government sought to use [[Anwar al-Awlaki]] ... as an informant, and that al-Awlaki tried unsuccessfully to lure Al-Timimi into illegal conduct as part of a government sting."<ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-07-19 |title=Some convictions overturned in terrorism case against Muslim scholar from Virginia |url=https://apnews.com/article/islamic-scholar-paintball-treason-conviction-overturned-timimi-a9479a25f9825a022ffe68f4a64d0fc5 |access-date=2024-09-02 |website=AP News |language=en}}</ref>

On August 1, 2025, Al-Timimi's direct appeal was filed in the Fourth Circuit after twenty years in the district court.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.courtlistener.com/docket/67420780/united-states-v-ali-al-timimi/|title=United States v. Ali Al-Timimi, 14-4451 - CourtListener.com|website=CourtListener}}</ref>

On January 9, 2026, the 4th Circuit Court of Appeals unanimously voted to overturn Al-Timimi's remaining convictions, finding that his statements were protected by the [[First Amendment to the United States Constitution|First Amendment]]. In the ruling, Circuit Judge [[James Andrew Wynn]] stated, "Ali al-Timimi was convicted based entirely on words he spoke in the immediate aftermath of the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks -- words that were inflammatory, disturbing and deeply offensive, but that urged no concrete criminal plan and did not provide operational assistance for the commission of any particular offense".<ref>{{Cite web|URL=https://www.upi.com/Top_News/US/2026/01/09/al-timimi-conviction-overturned/2121767992831/|title=Appeals court overturns conviction of accused terrorism recruiter|work=UPI|date=January 9, 2026|access-date=January 11, 2026}}</ref><ref name=Politico/><ref>{{Cite web |date=2026-01-09 |title=No. 14-4451 |url=https://www.ca4.uscourts.gov/opinions/144451.P.pdf |access-date=2026-01-20 |format=PDF |publisher=United States Court Of Appeals For The Fourth Circuit |language=en-US}}</ref>

==Judgment of Acquittal==
On March 3, 2026, Judge Brinkema "ORDERED and ADJUDGED that the defendant, Ali Al-Timimi, is fully acquitted, discharged, and any bond exonerated as to ALL COUNTS as charged in the Superseding Indictment (Dkt 47)."<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=16788129116690087542&q=ali+al-timimi&hl=en&as_sdt=3,47|title=United States v. AL-TIMIMI, Dist. Court, ED Virginia 2026 - Google Scholar}}</ref>
